passage_title: Smoke-Water and Cold Storage in Mirelle Seed Germination
passage:
Mirelle is a wildflower whose seeds often fail to sprout. Botanists tested two treatments: soaking seeds in smoke-water (water through which smoke from burned plants has been bubbled, then diluted) and storing seeds in a cold, moist place before planting.

In every trial, 200 seeds were soaked for 24 hours, then planted on moist paper at 18°C. After 21 days, the botanists recorded the percent of seeds that germinated and the mean number of days until germination (see Table 1).

Experiment 1
Seeds were soaked in plain water (none) or in smoke-water diluted 1:1,000, 1:100, or 1:10, then planted with no cold storage.

Experiment 2
Seeds were soaked as in Experiment 1, stored at 4°C for 6 weeks, then planted.

Experiment 3
Seeds were soaked in 1:100 smoke-water and stored at 4°C for 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8 weeks before planting. (The 0-week result is that of Experiment 1 and the 6-week result is that of Experiment 2 for 1:100.)
prompt: In Experiment 1, germination was highest with which soaking treatment?
subskill: locate a maximum within one series
topic_tag: Smoke-Water and Cold Storage in Mirelle Seed Germination

graphic.caption: Table 1. Germination of Mirelle seeds after 21 days

consistency_check: Germination never exceeds 61% and moves opposite to mean days in each series; the strongest smoke-water depresses germination without cold but not after it (interaction); storage gains level off after 6 weeks; shared trials (1:100 at 0 and 6 weeks) have identical values across experiments.

passage:
In the Harl Valley, numbers of Dunmore voles rise for 3 years and then fall sharply in the 4th year. This 4-year cycle has been recorded for 40 years. In a peak year, voles reach about 300 per hectare; after a crash, about 20 per hectare remain. Ermines (small predators) eat voles, and voles feed mainly on cotton sedge, a grasslike plant. Three scientists explain the crash.

Scientist 1
Predators cause the crash. When voles are plentiful, more young ermines survive, so ermine numbers lag vole numbers by about 1 year: ermines are most numerous in the year after voles peak. By then, ermines eat voles faster than voles can reproduce. The crash begins in late summer, when that year's young ermines start to hunt. Voles in a fenced plot that keeps ermines out would not crash. The condition of the sedge does not affect vole breeding.

Scientist 2
The sedge causes the crash. After voles have eaten more than half of the sedge leaves in an area for two summers in a row, the sedge grows leaves rich in silica the following spring. Silica-rich leaves wear down voles' teeth and provide little nourishment, so females stop breeding. Sedge leaves in a crash year contain about 3 times as much silica as usual. The crash begins in spring. Voles in a fenced plot that keeps ermines out would still crash.

Scientist 3
Crowding causes the crash. When vole numbers first exceed about 250 per hectare, females fight over nest sites; stressed females produce fewer young, and many young die in the nest. The crash begins whenever this density is first passed, in any season. The sedge stays nutritious throughout the cycle, so food is not involved. Voles in a plot kept below 250 per hectare by removing voles would not crash, even with ermines present.
prompt: Which scientist(s) would predict that a crash begins in spring?
explanation: Scientist 2 says "The crash begins in spring." Scientist 1 says late summer, and Scientist 3 says whenever density first passes 250, in any season. So "Scientist 2 only".
domain: Evaluation of Models, Inferences, and Experimental Results
subskill: locate a prediction in the viewpoints
consistency_check: Each scientist predicts a different season (late summer / spring / whenever density passes 250) and a different fenced-plot outcome; ermine lag of 1 year puts the ermine peak in year 4, after the year-3 vole peak.

passage_title: Why the Cawl Ridge Springs Are Warm
passage:
Water flowing from the Cawl Ridge springs averages 34°C. Rainwater at the site averages 9°C, and ordinary groundwater from a well 1 km away is 11°C. The springs' flow rises about 2 months after the start of each wet season. Three scientists explain why the springs are warm.

Scientist 1
Rainwater sinks along a crack in the rock (a fault) to a depth of about 2 km, where the rock is warm, and then rises back to the surface. The round trip takes about 2 months, which is why flow rises about 2 months after the wet season starts. Because the deep rock stays at the same temperature all year, the water's temperature does not change with the flow. On its long trip, the water dissolves minerals, so it should carry about 900 milligrams of dissolved salts per liter (mg/L).

Scientist 2
A body of hot rock lies only about 300 m below the springs. Rainwater that reaches the hot rock is heated and rises within a few days. The 2-month delay in flow is caused by a layer of clay above the hot rock that slows rainwater on its way down. Gas bubbling out of the springs should contain sulfur gases released by the hot rock.

Scientist 3
Rainwater seeps down to a layer of granite about 600 m deep. This granite is unusually rich in elements that release heat, so it warms the water that flows past it. The longer the water stays in contact with the granite, the warmer it becomes, so the springs should be warmest in the months when flow is lowest.
prompt: Which scientist(s) would predict that the temperature of the spring water changes as the flow rate changes?
explanation: Scientist 3 says slower flow means warmer water. Scientist 1 says the temperature does not change with the flow, and Scientist 2 does not connect temperature to flow. So "Scientist 3 only".
domain: Evaluation of Models, Inferences, and Experimental Results
subskill: locate a prediction in the viewpoints
topic_tag: Why the Cawl Ridge Springs Are Warm
consistency_check: Depths are consistent with each claim (2 km, 300 m, 600 m); only Scientist 3 ties temperature to flow; only Scientist 1 predicts dissolved salts (900 mg/L); 34 - 11 = 23 and 34 - 9 = 25.

passage_title: Why the Cawl Ridge Springs Are Warm
passage:
Water flowing from the Cawl Ridge springs averages 34°C. Rainwater at the site averages 9°C, and ordinary groundwater from a well 1 km away is 11°C. The springs' flow rises about 2 months after the start of each wet season. Three scientists explain why the springs are warm.

Scientist 1
Rainwater sinks along a crack in the rock (a fault) to a depth of about 2 km, where the rock is warm, and then rises back to the surface. The round trip takes about 2 months, which is why flow rises about 2 months after the wet season starts. Because the deep rock stays at the same temperature all year, the water's temperature does not change with the flow. On its long trip, the water dissolves minerals, so it should carry about 900 milligrams of dissolved salts per liter (mg/L).

Scientist 2
A body of hot rock lies only about 300 m below the springs. Rainwater that reaches the hot rock is heated and rises within a few days. The 2-month delay in flow is caused by a layer of clay above the hot rock that slows rainwater on its way down. Gas bubbling out of the springs should contain sulfur gases released by the hot rock.

Scientist 3
Rainwater seeps down to a layer of granite about 600 m deep. This granite is unusually rich in elements that release heat, so it warms the water that flows past it. The longer the water stays in contact with the granite, the warmer it becomes, so the springs should be warmest in the months when flow is lowest.
prompt: A test hole is drilled near the springs to a depth of 350 m. Which scientist(s) would most likely predict that the rock at the bottom of the hole is warmer than 34°C?
explanation: Scientist 2 places hot rock about 300 m below the springs, so a 350-m hole would reach it. Scientist 3's granite is about 600 m deep, and Scientist 1's warm rock is about 2 km deep. So "Scientist 2 only".
